newsitem.title: KENYA: Barclays Kenya sells holding to insurance firm.
newsitem.headline: Barclays Kenya sells holding to insurance firm.

text.p: Barclays Bank of Kenya on Thursday sold its 11 percent holding in investment company National Industrial Credit to the Insurance Company of East Africa (ICEA), brokers said.

They said the 4,827,295 shares in National Industrial Credit shares were sold at 45 shillings per share in the biggest single transaction on the Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE) since its inception in 1954.
National Industrial Credit gained 50 cents on the ordinary floor to 40.50 on conclusion of the deal on the three-day special lots board while Barclays dropped a shilling to 98.
Insurance Company of East Africa is not listed on the NSE.
A spokesman at the insurance firm confirmed the purchase.
He said the firm already owned some 12.5 percent of National Industrial Credit and its stake would rise to 23.5 percent.
The spokesman said ICEA would pay for the shares in cash.
"We have to pay tomorrow (Friday)," the spokesman added. "We have held a substantial shareholding in that company and it is only logical that we consolidate our position."
The Insurance Company of East Africa is a subsidiary of First Chartered Securities, which has vast interests ranging from real estate, maritime business, insurance and banking.
Brokers said National Industrial Credit outperformed any other stock in the financial sector in the last year, when the market was on average depressed.
A trader said given dividends and a one-for-four bonus it offered last year, the National Industrial Credit stock's performance in the bourse was "relatively very good".
Barclays had offered the National Industrial Credit shares on the special lots board at 52 shillings each but a final deal at the 45-shilling price was above its current level.
"The deal carries a premium. Today, National Industrial Credit closed at 40.50 on the ordinary floor; this makes a premium of around 10 percent," a leading broker said.
"That is not abnormal in this market or an international market. This is not unreasonable given the huge block of shares traded," the broker told Reuters.
Investment advisers said National Industrial Credit's trading price, adjusted for the dividend and bonus, showed gains since flotation.

But an official at a leading brokerage house told Reuters many domestic Kenyan investors simply looked at the current share price and were unhappy it appeared in the 40-shilling range compared to its price of 52 on flotation in 1994.

"Many investors still have a simple understanding of the exchange. They look at the prices offered on the bourse and decide they are making losses," a floor dealer said. "But with the dividend and bonus, the share is at a premium."

The shares Barclays sold were those left when it offered to sell 51 percent of its holding in 1994. Brokers said Barclays was moving out because National Industrial Credit's plans to enter banking would be in conflict with its core business.
($1=56 shillings).
